title: US Lawmaker Seeks to Name India in Russia Sanctions Bill Authorizing 100% Tariffs
excerpt: Democratic Congressman Steny Hoyer's amendment would explicitly list India among ten countries eligible for up to 100% duties, as the House races a four-day clock before its pre-midterm recess.
body:
• Democratic Congressman Steny Hoyer has submitted a House amendment that would explicitly name China, India, Turkiye, Azerbaijan, Hungary, the Slovak Republic, the UAE, Singapore, Kazakhstan, and the Kyrgyz Republic as eligible for duties of up to 100% under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.
  • The Senate passed the bill 86–11 on Aug. 7 without naming any country — it refers only to the five largest importers of Russian oil and gas by volume — so explicit naming would be a substantive change.
  • A rival amendment proposes scrapping the tariff section altogether, setting up a fight over the bill's sharpest weapon as the House faces four working days before an early recess ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
  • India imported a record 2.7 million barrels per day of Russian crude in June — more than half its total crude imports — making it the second-largest buyer after China, according to CREA data reported by PTI.

What happened

Racing against the clock, U.S. lawmakers have submitted amendments to the Russia sanctions bill — one seeking to explicitly name its top trading partners, including India, in the legislation, and another proposing to scrap the section imposing tariffs altogether, PTI reported.

The amendment moved by Democratic Congressman Steny Hoyer seeks to name China, India, Turkiye, Azerbaijan, Hungary, the Slovak Republic, the UAE, Singapore, Kazakhstan, and the Kyrgyz Republic as countries eligible for 100% duties. The flurry of amendments comes as the House has just four working days left before it breaks into an early recess ahead of the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Context and background

The underlying measure, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, passed the U.S. Senate on Aug. 7 by an overwhelming 86–11 vote. It seeks to impose sanctions not only on Russia's leadership and energy sector but also on the "shadow fleet" of vessels that enable Moscow to evade sanctions on oil deliveries. Washington believes Russia's crude oil trade is funding the war against Ukraine.

The bill is named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, its longtime author and champion. It authorizes President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on Russia's top oil trading partners. Crucially, the Senate-passed version does not name those partners — it refers to the five largest importers of oil and gas by volume. Hoyer's amendment would replace that formula with an explicit list.

Earlier drafts were far harsher: the original carried a blanket 500% tariff threat, later eased to a maximum of 100% on the top five purchasers, Reuters reported. The bill also builds in executive discretion — the president "shall" raise duties "up to" 100%, a ceiling rather than a mandate — plus waivers deemed in the U.S. national interest.

Impact and analysis

Naming countries explicitly would strip away the ambiguity that has so far let New Delhi argue over whether it falls inside the penalty box. India is the second-largest buyer of Russian hydrocarbons after China — CREA data cited by PTI put June imports at EUR 5.5 billion, including a record 2.7 million barrels per day of crude, more than half of India's total crude imports. A 100% U.S. tariff would hit Indian exporters hard and force refiners to weigh cheap Russian cargoes against access to the American market.

But the tariff remains a weapon, not an inevitability. The bill creates an enabling framework: it must still clear the House, win Trump's signature, and survive the executive branch's waiver discretion — and the rival amendment to delete the tariff section altogether shows the House is far from settled. Fifteen European countries that buy small, shrinking volumes of Russian gas could qualify for exemptions under the volume-based criteria, according to reports — an escape hatch that explicit naming could close for the listed ten.

The diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora in the United States, the fight sits at the intersection of two loyalties: American consumers and businesses watching energy and trade policy, and Indian exporters — textiles, pharmaceuticals, gems, and IT services — whose U.S. market access could become collateral in the Russia dispute. Indian-American investors and business owners with supply chains running through India will be watching the House markup closely, since the difference between Hoyer's named list and a scrapped tariff section is the difference between a defined threat and an avoided one.

What to watch next

The immediate question is whether the House acts at all before its pre-midterm recess — four working days is a narrow window for a bill with competing amendments. If the House passes the measure, it goes to Trump; if it stalls, the tariff threat dies with the calendar. Either way, the amendment fight has put India explicitly on the legislative map.
